narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Chandor, originally Chandrapur, was the capital of the Kadamba dynasty.
The dance is linked to King Harihara I of the Vijayanagara Empire, who reportedly performed it in 1390 after defeating a Chola ruler.
It also commemorates the fall of the Yadav dynasty.

Image — MISSING

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally a Shigmo tradition, it is now performed on the second day of the Goa Carnival.
It serves as an artistic commemoration of historical victories and the Kadamba period.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers form two rows and march to a specific beat, later forming a circle to simulate grain pounding with pestles.
A lead dancer holds a leash attached to a participant in a bear costume.
The routine includes a symbolic sweeping of the ground by a Devadasi girl.
Watch for Pounding.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music is provided by the ghumot, kansaalle (jhanjh), and dholke.
The pestles themselves are instruments, containing internal bells or blades.
Listen for the Ghumot, Kansaalle, Jhanjh, Dholke.
The sound is dominated by the earthy resonance of the ghumot drum and the metallic jingling of the pestles' internal blades as they strike the ground.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Performers wear a dhoti, long-sleeved shirt, black jacket, and a turban (pagdi).
The dance occurs in front of the village church and in the yards of local houses, accompanied by torchbearers called divtekars.

scenes.title: The people
narration: King Harihara I of the Vijayanagara Empire is cited as a historical performer of the dance in 1390.
The dance is specifically preserved in the village of Chandor in the Salcete region of Goa.
The dance claims lineage from the Satavahana and Kadamba dynasties, with influences from the Vijayanagara Empire.
